newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Air NZ-Ansett deal heroic but painful, say analysts.
newsitem.headline: Air NZ-Ansett deal heroic but painful, say analysts.

text.p: Air New Zealand's buy-in to Australia's Ansett Holdings was seen by analysts on Tuesday as strategically heroic but financially painful.
The NZ$540 million (US$373 million) outlay for half of Ansett was a necessary precursor to becoming a significant regional player and would open a route to participation in a global airline group.
"Five or three years down the track Air New Zealand are going to look like heroes. Short-term, there is probably likely to be some pain," said SBC Warburg analyst Timothy Ross.
"Without this deal they are a bit player, and with it they are a significant regional player with the capacity to participate in a major international airline grouping," he said.
Air NZ will buy 50 percent of Ansett from transport group TNT Ltd. Rupert Murdoch's News Corp owns the other half.
Peter Harbison, Managing Director for Sydney's Centre for Asia-Pacific Aviation, called the news "one of the major milestones in Australia-New Zealand aviation".
"This is the beginning of the single aviation market. It's a major, logical step that everyone has been waiting for for years ever since deregulation came in in Australia and New Zealand.'

People would be able to do business as easily from Sydney to Auckland as to Cairns. It opened the possibility to link many different gateways, as was being pioneered by New Zealand budget carrier Kiwi Air.
"It will dramatically change the way we do business and take holidays," Harbison said. "Within five years we will have the melding of the two domestic markets."

The simultaneous move by the New Zealand government to allow foreigners to own 49 percent of Air NZ via its 'B' shares, from 35 percent previously, would eventually open the group for a major foreign stake holder, almost certainly an airline.
It would also, said Cavill White analyst David Copley, make it easier for Brierley Investments, 42 percent owner of Air NZ, to quit part of its holding in a more liquid market.
Harbison said the Ansett-Air New Zealand alliance was a very attractive partnership. Front runners among many suitors would be Singapore Airlines and Malaysian Airline System Bhd.

"That's one of the fundamental reasons for the equity alliance -- it's a world aviation market now and you have to be involved in a global aviation alliance. Qantas is in one and Air New Zealand has to be in one," said Copley.
Ross sees eventual marriage with United-Thai-Lufthansa or some other major U.S.-European-Asian grouping.
Air NZ would strengthen Ansett in Australia where it has lost market share and yield because of ownership uncertainties.
A A$200 million (US$158 million) capital injection and Air NZ's aggressive bottom-line-driven approach would revitalise Ansett, he said.
However, Ross does not expect any turnaround to be easy.
"Neither TNT nor News have been able to turn Ansett around over the last couple of years, so the onus is definitely on Air New Zealand management to jump into the cockpit," he said.
"The ability to be able to spread themselves over what is now a fairly large empire.
He has other qualms -- whether Ansett has skeletons in the cupboard and over Australia's "recalcitrant labour practices".
But his main worry is near the half billion dollar price paid for an asset that in 96/97 is only forecast to break even.
"There is a possible risk that restructuring might result in the costs exceeding the benefits in the short-term."
Air NZ said the deal is profit-neutral in the short term but Ross has raised his 1996/97 profit forecast by NZ$5 million to NZ$235 million against NZ$225 million in the year to June 1996.
Despite many rumours of quitting, the main rival to Ansett-Air NZ, Qantas, retains 19.9 percent of Air NZ.

Copley said the first indication of what it will do with its holding will come when it has to stump up with NZ$48 million to participate in its share of the 3/11 Air NZ rights issue announced as part of the deal.

Air NZ's B shares dived 38 cents to NZ$3.95 on the news due to the diluting effect of the increased foreign ownership rules, but the A shares, only able to be held by New Zealanders, were up 11 cents at NZ$3.25 in late trade.
